title: Complex-looking yet computationally reducible systems are very rare

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complex-looking yet computationally reducible systems are very rare

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Systems whose behavior looks complex but is nevertheless computationally reducible, such as the cellular automaton that generates digits of powers of 2, are very rare; in the vast majority of cases complex-looking behavior in nature and elsewhere is computationally irreducible.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I strongly suspect that systems like this are very rare, and that in the vast majority of cases where the behavior that we see in nature and elsewhere appears to us complex it is in the end indeed associated with computational irreducibility.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Computational Irreducibility” (from p. 737), p. 748. Scope: systems with complex-looking behavior in nature and among simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.39

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A restricted frequency claim can be tested in public enumerations. The stated vast-majority conclusion across nature and all systems has no defined sampling frame, so available evidence cannot resolve it as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Choose explicit ensembles of programs and natural models, define visual complexity and computational reducibility, and estimate the frequency of complex-looking reducible members. High frequencies in representative ensembles refute rarity there; low frequencies plus certified predictors or lower bounds support it only for those ensembles.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Appearance of complexity is observer- and metric-dependent.

Natural systems are not adequately represented by program catalogs.

There is no canonical probability distribution over all systems.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.3
discriminating power: 0.35
data adequacy: 0.2
analysis feasibility: 0.35

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public simulators can enumerate small rule spaces and compare apparent complexity with known shortcuts, which is a proxy for the simple-program half. Very rare, and the vast majority of complex-looking natural behavior, presume a measure the text does not give. Irreducibility of a natural process is not settled by the look of a picture.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate simple programs up to a size bound, flag outputs that standard compressors leave incompressible, and test whether a short map from position to color still exists. A high rate of such shortcuts would challenge rarity among programs; natural systems still require their actual rules.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Looks complex depends on a perceptual or compression criterion the claim leaves open.

A missing shortcut is compatible with a shortcut not yet found.

Natural systems sit outside the enumerable set of simple programs.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.35
